# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** A phylogenetic distance model estimates the expected number of substitutions separating two aligned sequences, including changes hidden by repeated mutation at the same site.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Biological question** | How evolutionarily separated are two homologous sequences? |
| **Computational problem** | Convert an observed fraction of aligned differences into a comparable distance despite unobserved substitutions |
| **Method type** | Stochastic substitution model and pairwise estimation |
| **Input** | Homologous multiple-sequence alignment, with a stated treatment of gaps and ambiguous bases |
| **Output** | Pairwise distance matrix, often used to infer a tree |
| **Prerequisites** | [Needleman--Wunsch global alignment](needleman-wunsch-global-alignment.qmd), [Smith--Waterman local alignment](smith-waterman-local-alignment.qmd), [neighbor-joining trees](neighbor-joining-trees.qmd) |

# Why mismatch fraction is not an evolutionary distance

For two aligned sequences, the *p-distance* is the fraction $p$ of comparable columns with different symbols. It is a useful descriptive quantity, but it is not generally the expected number of substitutions per site. A site can mutate from A to G and later from G to A; the observed bases then match even though two changes occurred. Different substitutions can also occur successively at one site, a phenomenon called **multiple hits**.

As sequences diverge, observed mismatch fraction saturates while actual evolutionary change continues. A distance model supplies a probabilistic relationship between the unobserved substitution process and the alignment. Its estimate is meaningful only relative to the model, alignment, and filtering choices used to obtain it.

```text
homologous alignment
       -> count comparable matching and differing columns
       -> fit / apply a substitution model
       -> corrected pairwise distances
       -> distance-based tree or exploratory analysis
```

# A simple correction: Jukes--Cantor

The Jukes--Cantor (JC69) model assumes four nucleotides have equal equilibrium frequencies and that every one-base change has the same instantaneous rate. Under those restrictive assumptions, the corrected distance is

$$
d_{\mathrm{JC69}}=-\frac{3}{4}\ln\left(1-\frac{4p}{3}\right).
$$

Here $p$ is the observed mismatch fraction and $d_{\mathrm{JC69}}$ is the estimated expected substitutions per site. For small $p$, $d$ is close to $p$. As $p$ approaches $0.75$, the logarithm becomes unstable: the alignment no longer contains enough information under this model to estimate a finite distance reliably.

## Toy example

If 8 of 100 comparable nucleotide columns differ, then $p=0.08$ and

$$
d_{\mathrm{JC69}}=-\frac{3}{4}\ln(1-4\times0.08/3)\approx0.085.
$$

The correction is modest because a second mutation at the same site is unlikely at this divergence. If 60 of 100 columns differ, the same calculation gives about $1.21$ substitutions per site, far larger than $0.60$; uncertainty and model misspecification are also much more consequential there.

# Models add biological realism

JC69 is often too simple for real DNA. More flexible models distinguish the changes and base compositions that data support.

| Model | Main extra feature | Typical use and caution |
|---|---|---|
| JC69 | Equal base frequencies and equal rates | Pedagogy or closely related sequences; rarely a sufficient final model |
| K80 / K2P | Separate transition and transversion rates | Useful when transition bias matters; still assumes equal base frequencies |
| F81 | Unequal equilibrium base frequencies | Addresses composition, but not transition bias |
| HKY85 | Unequal frequencies plus transition/transversion bias | Common interpretable DNA model |
| GTR | A distinct reversible rate for each substitution pair | Flexible baseline; needs enough information and is often combined with rate heterogeneity |

Sites do not necessarily evolve at one rate. A gamma-distributed rate model ($+\Gamma$), a proportion of invariant sites, or an explicit codon/protein model can better match a dataset. These additions are models of an average process; they do not repair poor homology, recombination, contamination, or a mixture of unrelated evolutionary histories.

# Estimating and using distances

For a fixed model, software can estimate a pairwise distance by maximizing the probability of the two sequences separated by a branch length. This uses all observed substitution categories, rather than only mismatch fraction. From $n$ taxa, the result is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix; diagonal entries are zero.

Distance methods such as [neighbor-joining trees](neighbor-joining-trees.qmd) use this matrix directly. The matrix is a lossy summary of the alignment: it is fast and useful, but it does not retain site-pattern information that likelihood- and Bayesian-tree methods use. When comparing distances, retain the alignment coordinates, model, gap policy, and any column filtering because changing them changes the estimate.

## Assumptions and diagnostics

| Issue | Why it matters | Practical response |
|---|---|---|
| Homologous alignment | Misaligned columns are treated as substitutions | Inspect alignment quality; align coding regions by codon where appropriate |
| One history across sites | Recombination can make one tree and its distances misleading | Screen or partition recombinant/heterogeneous regions |
| Adequate model | Composition bias and rate variation distort branch lengths | Compare plausible models and report the selected one |
| Moderate divergence | Saturation erases historical signal | Examine distances and use richer data/markers rather than overinterpreting large corrections |
| Independent sampling | Duplicate or contaminated sequences can dominate apparent similarity | Curate taxon identity, metadata, and sequence quality |

Gaps and ambiguous bases require an explicit policy. Pairwise deletion uses all usable columns for each pair but makes pairs based on different site sets; complete deletion uses one common set but may discard much information. Neither is universally right, and both should be reported.

# Connections and method choice

Distance models begin after an alignment has defined which residues are compared. They provide the matrix that [neighbor-joining trees](neighbor-joining-trees.qmd) converts into an unrooted tree. Tree topology alone is not a biological conclusion: bootstrap or other resampling assessments, alternative alignments, and model sensitivity should accompany it.

| Goal | Good starting point | Important limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Quick visualization of many related sequences | Model-corrected distances plus neighbor joining | Pairwise compression loses site-pattern information |
| Very close sequences | p-distance or simple correction | Still verify alignment and coverage comparability |
| Deeply divergent nucleotide sequences | Composition- and rate-aware model; consider amino acids/codons | Saturation and alignment uncertainty can remain limiting |
| Gene with recombination | Partition or use a recombination-aware analysis | One distance matrix cannot represent several local histories |

# Take-home Messages

1. Observed differences undercount substitutions when sites experience repeated mutation.
2. A distance is a model-based estimate, not a property of a sequence pair alone.
3. Transition bias, base composition, and among-site rate variation motivate models beyond JC69.
4. Distance matrices are fast, useful inputs to tree algorithms, but they discard alignment-level information and depend on sound homology and model choices.
